items.title: Preservice teachers’ professional judgement in GenAI-supported lesson planning
items.abstract: Lesson planning asks preservice teachers to consider how lesson aims, activities, and assessment fit together. Generative AI (GenAI) can now offer a complete draft in which many of these choices have already been made. Studies have examined the quality of generated plans and how preservice teachers prompt, evaluate, and revise them. Yet less is known about the educational rationale behind specific choices in a generated plan. This qualitative study explores how professional judgement becomes visible when preservice teachers use GenAI to plan lessons. We analysed interviews with six preservice teachers in China alongside the planning materials they provided. Participants considered curriculum requirements, classroom feasibility, anticipated teaching, and anticipated student responses when judging GenAI suggestions. Their reasons varied across planning episodes and within individual plans. At times, they examined an example or activity closely while offering little explanation for a lesson structure they had retained. These accounts suggest that an apparently complete plan may draw attention to some decisions while leaving others less closely examined. The findings point to the value of keeping lesson aims, sequence, learner activity, and assessment open to professional judgement during teacher preparation.

items.title: PRESERVING STUDENTS' METACOGNITIVE AGENCY IN AI-ASSISTED EFL WRITING INSTRUCTION: A PEDAGOGICAL FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: The inevitable integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English language teaching has transformed traditional approaches to writing instruction. Although AI offers numerous opportunities for improving students’ writing skills through immediate feedback, language correction, and personalized support, its increasing use raises concerns about students’ ability to think and work independently. In particular, excessive reliance on AI may reduce students’ active engagement in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their own writing. Therefore, the question is not whether AI should be integrated into EFL writing instruction, but how teachers can use it without weakening students’ metacognitive agency. Drawing on recent research, this paper discusses the importance of maintaining students’ responsibility for their learning and proposes the Metacognitive Agency Preservation and Development (MAPD) Framework. The framework introduces five stages of AI-assisted writing instruction aimed at encouraging independent thinking, critical evaluation, and reflective learning. It emphasizes that AI should support students throughout the writing process rather than replace their cognitive efforts. The paper concludes that the effective integration of AI requires a balance between technological assistance and students’ independent metacognitive development.

items.title: Principles for the ethical implementation of automated welfare monitoring in animal research: The 3Rs and beyond
items.abstract: Automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being implemented in animal research, particularly through Automated Welfare Monitoring (AWM) systems designed to augment traditional human assessment of animal welfare. Among the most prominent examples are home cage monitoring technologies for continuous monitoring of rodents. Current ethical discussions surrounding AWM primarily focus on its contribution to the 3Rs principles (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), especially its potential to minimise harm through continuous welfare assessment and earlier interventions. However, the 3Rs alone do not fully address the broader ethical and social implications of automation and AI in animal research. AWM systems have the potential to reshape decision-making, responsibility, oversight, animal care jobs, and human-animal relationships within laboratory practice. In this article, we propose a complementary framework for the ethical implementation of AWM in animal research. Drawing on scholarship in bioethics and AI ethics, we propose five principles to guide the design, implementation, and governance of AWM systems: (1) Animal Welfare and 3Rs; (2) Human Autonomy and Accountability; (3) Fairness; (4) Transparency; and (5) Respect for Animals. We illustrate how these principles address ethical concerns arising from AWM, including the preservation of professional expertise and autonomy, equitable access across institutions and species, data governance and regulatory oversight, and the risks of objectifying animals through datafication. Rather than replacing the 3Rs, these principles extend them by addressing the ethical and social conditions under which automated systems are integrated into animal research, thereby supporting the responsible implementation of AWM while promoting animal welfare.

items.title: Prompt Design and Automated Assessment: A Comparative Evaluation of Claude and ChatGPT Against Teacher Marking of Handwritten Examinations
items.abstract: This study compares Claude and ChatGPT against teacher marking of handwritten Psychology examination scripts, examining how prompt design affects large language models (LLMs)–human agreement. Sixty-nine handwritten scripts, as photographic images, were graded by both LLMs under four prompting strategies (minimal, rubric, exemplar, role-based). Both LLMs differed significantly from the teacher in seven of eight conditions; Claude under role-based prompting was the sole exception (p = 0.038). ChatGPT overmarked across all four prompts, while Claude’s deviation varied across prompt conditions. Prompt type had a significant impact on grading accuracy with a significant LLM × Prompt interaction (p = 0.001, η²p = 0.08). Claude under the exemplar prompt had the closest agreement with the teacher’s marks (MAE = 2.42; r = 0.84). A grade-level analysis showed that scoring accuracy did not always result in grade-level agreement, indicating both metrics are needed. Prompt design improved LLM grading accuracy, but neither model reproduced teachers’ marks closely enough to replace human oversight in high-stakes assessment.

items.title: Psychological Readiness for the Green Energy Transition: A Human-Factors Model for Aviation Maintenance Crews
items.abstract: Green-aviation research on battery and alternative-fuel chemistries has advanced rapidly, but a persistent blind spot remains: the psychological readiness of the maintenance personnel who operate these systems daily under safety-critical conditions.Silver-zinc (Ag-Zn) batteries, used in fighter aircraft for their high energy density, evolve hydrogen and oxygen gas through electrolysis of their alkaline electrolyte during charging -a hazard that builds invisibly over 36-to-72-hour charge cycles and becomes dangerous only once hydrogen concentration crosses its lower explosion limit.Managing this hazard depends less on chemistry knowledge and more on sustained technician vigilance during a long, low-stimulation monitoring task -precisely the condition under which classic vigilancedecrement research shows attentional lapses emerge, independent of training or competence.Drawing on the author's two decades as an aviation electrical maintenance engineer and a second career in applied and clinical psychology within the same defence environment, this paper argues that emerging green-energy-storage chemistries (lithium-ion, solidstate, hydrogen fuel cells) will introduce comparable low-visibility, highconsequence hazards, and that maintenance-crew psychological readiness must be engineered alongside the chemistry itself.Integrating self-efficacy theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and vigilance-decrement research, the paper proposes a Psychology-Chemistry Interface Model with three components -chemistry-literacy calibration, hazardtolerability screening, and stress-buffered reporting culture -and a training framework for building calibrated, sustained vigilance in ground crews adopting new energy chemistries, including a low-cost toolkit -a pre-task hazard card, a vigilance-rotation roster, a hazard-tolerability selfcheck, and an added prompt within existing incident-reporting procedures -deployable at a single maintenance unit without new infrastructure.

items.title: Public health talent development in the AI era: a framework for sustainable Sino-African collaboration
items.abstract: Background While Sino-African higher education cooperation is expanding, it is unclear whether and to what degree short-term programs (e.g., scholarships) have consistently translated into progress, such as sustainable growth at the individual, institutional, and societal levels in both China and Africa, particularly in the era of artificial intelligence (AI). Both the pandemic and AI have transformed public-health education, research, and practice while introducing unprecedented issues regarding data governance, algorithmic bias, privacy, and technological inequity. However, there is a dearth of theoretical insights on sustainable Sino-African cooperation, particularly in the context of public health talent development in the AI era. To bridge this gap, this study aims to investigate how resources and capabilities can be transformed into sustainable, reciprocal public-health talent development. Methods An integrative review was conducted following the five stages proposed by Whittemore and Knafl in 2005: problem identification, literature search, data evaluation, data analysis, and findings presentation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines informed the processes of evidence identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and synthesis. Heterogeneous evidence concerning China–Africa cooperation, public-health talent development, AI and digital health, knowledge co-creation, institutionalization, and responsible AI governance was critically evaluated and synthesized across micro-, meso-, and macro-levels of Sino-African collaborations. Results A total of 11 articles met the eligibility criteria. Based on detailed analysis of the evidence, the China–Africa Transformative AI Logistics & Young Scientist Talent System (CATALYST) was developed. The framework positions young public-health talents as both the central developmental outcome and active agents of collaboration. At the micro level, equitable capability and resource co-creation support talent development; at the meso level, reciprocity, trust, and knowledge co-creation facilitate translation into education, research, policy, and practice; and at the macro level, institutional mechanisms enable sustained system-level cooperation. AI functions as both an enabling technology and a domain requiring responsible governance. Conclusion The CATALYST framework provides a theoretically grounded pathway from resource sharing to knowledge co-creation and ecosystem-building, offering a foundation for designing sustainable, reciprocal, and ethically governed China–Africa public-health talent-development initiatives and for subsequent empirical validation.

items.title: Public support for AI environmental policies in Japan and South Korea-Inputs for adaptive governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to environmental sustainability while causing environmental problems. From the perspective of adaptive governance, we ask what the governments of Japan and South Korea would have to learn from their publics at the initial stage of adaptation. Using a 2024 survey of 700 citizens in each country, we find public support for a firm-targeted subsidy and a tax, with the tax receiving more support in both countries. Support was associated with concern about climate change and AI, and with anticipated environmental effectiveness. Trust in government was associated with subsidy support in Japan; no other trust association survived sensitivity analysis. Anticipated negative economic impact was associated with stronger tax support, though on a different time horizon in each country. We argue that support reaches further toward coercive instruments than innovation-first governance assumes, and that learning from it would require institutionalized citizen inputs and information on policy effects.

items.title: Quantifying impact and innovation in scientific publications: A structural–semantic framework combining co-authorship and research topics in Italian computer science
items.abstract: Traditional bibliometric indicators often fail to capture the multidimensional nature of scientific contributions, reducing complex intellectual identities to simple numerical scores. This study introduces a structural-semantic framework designed to quantify impact and innovation by integrating collaboration patterns with research topics. We model the complete population of 1,229 Italian computer science scholars using a hybrid 896-dimensional representation space. Our methodology combines structural graph embeddings derived from co-authorship networks with semantic representations of publication abstracts, utilizing transformer-based models and density-based clustering. To enhance interpretability, we employ a two-stage pipeline using large language models to generate scientifically coherent labels for identified research themes. Our integrated approach captures academic identity, paving the way for the creation a quantitative measure of research similarity. The framework successfully distinguishes researcher roles—such as specialists and interdisciplinary connectors and identified over 100 potential collaboration opportunities between researchers with shared expertise but no prior history of working together. Longitudinal analysis revealed three distinct waves of innovation in the Italian computer science landscape over the past 40 years, shifting from foundational theoretical infrastructure to applied artificial intelligence and health informatics. Furthermore, the model showed high predictive validity in forecasting future research interests. This framework provides a robust tool for science policy and institutional planning, offering a more faithful representation of scientific evolution than traditional citation-based metrics.

items.title: Questioning AI: Four Perspectives
items.abstract: In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. Building on his course, AI and Its Applications in the LIS Profession-- one of the few LIS offerings that comprehensively examines artificial intelligence and generative AI across libraries, archives, and museums; along with examining the historical, ethical, and sociopolitical dimensions of AI-- Simmons will highlight the importance of AI fluency in LIS, emphasizing practical, day-to-day applications for information professionals. He will introduce effective prompting strategies to support LIS workflows, including the TAP method (Think, Ask, Play), a framework he developed. Grounded in evidence-based iterative prompting this approach has produced positive outcomes through in-class experimentation with students. Laura Saunders teaches and writes in the areas of public services, reference, library instruction and information literacy. Drawing on scholarship and a critical pedagogy/ andragogy background, she will outline some AI skills and knowledge that might be important to address in these courses, explore how traditional skills such as the reference interview and neutral questioning remain relevant, and discuss how to highlight that continuity for students. She will also explore some of the pushback to AI content and share ideas for approaching AI assignments that preserves some student agency. Sarah Appedu is a PhD candidate whose dissertation research and teaching takes an agency and ethics-oriented approach to critically interrogating AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon. While access to AI tools and skills is often prioritized in many AI literacy initiatives, Sarah empowers librarians to ask the hard questions that go beyond issues of access and consider the ways in which AI can be in conflict with the very values we’re trained to embody. Her work aims to problematize the inevitability narratives surrounding AI use that are often perpetuated by the technology industry by centering librarians’ commitments to sustainability, the public good, equity, and intellectual freedom & property. She will present sets of critical questions related to each core value of librarianship that enable both technical knowledge of AI systems and agentic responses to their possibilities, limitations, and ethical consequences. The panelists will have several questions prompts prepared to help facilitate the conversation: Do LIS faculty have a need or obligation to integrate AI into their curricula? Why or why not? Have you experienced pressure either to integrate or to avoid AI in your teaching? Are you currently addressing AI in your teaching? If so, what activities, strategies or topics have you found to be effective? If not, what are your reasons for not addressing it? What are your experiences around student use of AI? What are your thoughts on AI inevitability and AI refusal? How can we navigate these tensions? The panel will be relevant to LIS instructors addressing or considering addressing AI in their curricula.

items.title: Reader Burden and Linguistic Register in AI-Generated Text: Implications for Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to prepare feedback, explanations and learning materials in higher education, raising a practical question beyond authorship: how suitable are these texts for the learners who read them? Four linked exploratory studies examine this question through perceived reader burden, defined as immediate feelings of fatigue and effort, alongside linguistic differences, source classification and computational rewriting. In a comparison involving 110 university students, an AI-generated news passage received a higher mean score than a human-written passage on an exploratory six-item reading-burden composite (3.20 vs. 2.05). To understand how these passages differed linguistically, the news pair was analysed alongside matched academic and blog pairs. Across all three, AI-generated passages showed higher lexical diversity, whereas readability and sentence-length variation followed less consistent patterns. The investigation then examined computational methods: logistic regression and an RBF-SVM achieved high accuracy in classifying text sources within their evaluation settings, whereas the RoBERTa-based detector achieved lower accuracy. Rewriting reduced heuristic scores but did not consistently produce coherent prose. Finally, an independent analysis of 60 cybersecurity passages found mixed linguistic patterns and limited success in recovering individual passages’ intended registers. Together, these findings suggest that reader burden, linguistic characteristics and source classification offer distinct forms of evidence rather than interchangeable indicators of educational suitability.

items.title: Recent Progress of Carbon Material-Based Flexible Sensors for Wearable Electronics
items.abstract: Wearable electronics have garnered considerable interest owing to their transformative potential in motion and health monitoring, artificial intelligence, human–machine interaction, and the Internet of Things. At the heart of these systems lie flexible sensors, including strain, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological devices, that serve as essential building blocks for wearable platforms. Among the diverse materials explored for such applications, carbonaceous materials, comprising carbon fibers, carbon nanotubes, graphene, and their derivatives, stand out as particularly attractive candidates by virtue of their superior electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, biocompatibility, and process compatibility with flexible substrates. Consequently, substantial research efforts have been directed toward the controlled synthesis and structural engineering of carbon materials to meet the stringent demands of next-generation electronics. This review provides an overview of recent progress in carbon-based flexible sensors, with emphasis on their classification and practical utility. Following a concise introduction to relevant carbon materials, the fundamental operating principles of typical flexible sensors, namely strain, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological sensors, are examined. Subsequently, their prominent applications in motion monitoring, human–machine interaction, and healthcare monitoring are critically discussed. The review concludes with an assessment of current challenges and future directions, aimed at guiding continued innovation in carbon-based flexible sensors for advanced wearable electronic systems.

items.title: Reconstructing Work Motivation of Pangkalan Data Pendidikan Tinggi (PDDIKTI) Operators in the Digital Transformation Era
items.abstract: Digital transformation in Islamic higher education has driven fundamental changes in academic data management systems, particularly regarding the role of PDDIKTI operators in Private Islamic Higher Education Institutions (PTKIS). The shift toward technology-based administrative systems demands improvements in digital literacy, work motivation, and organizational readiness to support accurate, efficient, and sustainable data management. This study aims to reconstruct the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators through a needs-and-expectations approach in the digital era, while identifying the psychological, technological, and organizational factors influencing operator performance. This study employs a literature review method analyzing 20 scientific articles published between 2022 and 2026, utilizing literature collection, selection, thematic grouping, and qualitative descriptive synthesis stages. The results indicate that digital transformation through academic information systems, e-learning, Dapodik, and the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) enhances work efficiency, service quality, and data accuracy. However, challenges persist, including low digital literacy, high administrative workloads, technological adaptation needs, and suboptimal organizational support. This study contributes to the development of a conceptual model that integrates motivational, technological, and managerial aspects as a foundation for understanding the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators in the era of digital transformation at PTKIS. The limitation of this study lies in its use of a literature review approach, meaning empirical data do not yet support the findings. Therefore, future research is recommended to conduct quantitative or qualitative empirical testing in the field to validate this conceptual model and to explore the effectiveness of organization-based digital literacy training programs in greater depth.

items.title: Redefining efficiency in post-editing of LLM-generated translation: why expert translators take more time
items.abstract: This study examines how expertise influences the post-editing of translation generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lens of relevant efficiency—the adaptive regulation of effort in response to task demands, which is operationalized here as temporal regulation, intervention calibration, and resource adaptability. We used keystroke logging and mixed-effects modeling to compare student and professional translators who performed full and light post-editing (FPE/LPE) tasks on LLM-generated translations under structured termbase and open-ended Internet-search settings. The findings suggest that post-editing expertise is not necessarily reflected in faster processing, but in how post-editing behavior relates to task requirements. Experts showed a greater increase in time allocation as the density of critical errors increased, indicating more task-sensitive temporal regulation. Expertise-related patterns of error correction varied with post-editing guidelines, while resource conditions were differentially associated with new-error introduction across the two groups. Keystroke-based process indicators also related to editing outcomes, highlighting the importance of evaluating editing activity in relation to its results. These findings support a task-relative understanding of relevant efficiency in the post-editing of LLM-generated translation, suggesting that translator training should prioritize task-sensitive decision-making, temporal regulation, and effective use of external resources rather than processing speed alone.

items.title: ReFTIR: Multitouch Sensing using FTIR Images Reconstructed based on Repropagated FTIR
items.abstract: Frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) has been used for contact sensing via vision, while repropagated FTIR (RFTIR) has enabled system miniaturization. However, conventional RFTIR-based methods cannot adequately handle overlapping contact images generated by multiple contacts. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach for estimating multiple contacts for multitouch sensing. Images resembling those captured by FTIR-based methods were reconstructed using pseudo-inverse ray tracing, and contact positions were then estimated based on these reconstructions. We evaluated the accuracy of multitouch sensing under various experimental conditions, and confirmed that the estimation was highly accurate, even with four contacts. Several applications were implemented to demonstrate the practicality of the proposed method, including single-sided and simultaneous double-sided multitouch sensing.

items.title: Regulation and Compliance with Building Regulations Research from 1990 to 2022: A Mixed-Method Review
items.abstract: Despite the importance of building regulations/codes/standards in the architecture, engineering, and construction industry, the characteristics of its regulation and compliance research are yet to be examined. This study addresses this knowledge gap. Adopting bibliometric, content, and scientometric analyses, as well as inferential statistics, a systematic review of enforcement and compliance with building regulations research from 1990 to 2022 was conducted. The five main research domains found are digital compliance, building energy efficiency and regulations compliance, and natural disaster mitigation through compliance. While there is a strong emphasis on compliance rate/levels and factors domain in various areas such as building daylight regulations, regulatory theories (with a focus on stakeholders and fire protection) have received minimal attention. A framework for future research directions is proposed. Overall, regulation and compliance theories, the benchmarking aspects of regulation, and fire safety require further research. Developed countries are research-active, and the developing ones are inactive. There are linear relationships; for example, as keyword occurrence increases, the total link strength between it and other keywords increases. The more papers journals publish, the more the average number of normalised citations received by the document they publish will increase. The study broadens the horizons of academics, policymakers, and regulators of artificial intelligence in digital compliance of building regulations and building energy efficiency in the climate change crisis. This study is the first detailed evidence and insight into the characteristics of compliance and enforcement of building regulations/codes/standards research. It is also the first of such research on the topic that adopts bibliometric and scientometric analyses, conducts an in-depth and sophisticated visualisation of the characteristics of the literature, and develops a framework for future research directions. Methodologically, the hybrid review methodology in this topic is novel, enabling the limitations of the traditional literature method to be mitigated by the analyses and the in-depth and sophisticated visualisation of the characteristics of the literature. Theoretically, there is extensive and scientific mapping of enforcement and compliance with building regulations research.

items.title: Regulatory evidentiary closure as a formal framework for citation faithfulness in large language models
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to generate answers with citations in regulatory settings, including compliance review, clinical governance, fiscal assessment, legal interpretation, and institutional risk analysis. Existing work on attribution, retrieval augmented generation, citation evaluation, and sufficient context has clarified when generated claims are grounded in identifiable sources. Regulatory use raises a stricter question. A citation may support an atomic sentence while still failing to justify the regulated conclusion that the system invites a user to accept. This paper develops regulatory evidentiary closure, a conclusion-relative standard for that question, as a formal framework. The framework defines source existence, domain-indexed claim support, and closure as relations over an authorized corpus, cited source set, generated claims, material elements, and regulated conclusion, and states them in explicit notation. Three propositions record the framework’s structure: claim support does not imply closure, metrics restricted to internal model signals cannot determine closure without domain rule structure, and closure checking reduces to a finite coverage problem over material elements. Worked examples from HIPAA security compliance and clinical guideline recommendation show the same failure structure across domains, where a citation supports an atomic claim while the conclusion’s material elements remain uncovered. A coverage matrix then maps seventeen existing evaluation methods against five evidentiary components and shows that none states conclusion-relative closure as an evaluation object. The paper translates the framework into a nine-step reviewer-facing audit protocol and identifies future work on element-mapping reliability, benchmark design, and tool-assisted closure assessment.

items.title: Reimagining Equity and Justice in the Digital Age: Legal Pathways for Societal Tranformation in the Twenty-First Century
items.abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping modern society, creating opportunities for development while simultaneously generating new forms of inequality, vulnerability and injustice. The study was undertaken because technological advancement does not automatically guarantee equitable participation, rights protection or access to justice, while existing legal responses to emerging digital challenges remain fragmented and largely reactive. The study aims to examine the relationship between digital transformation, equity and justice; analyse the theoretical and legal foundations for addressing emerging digital challenges; and develop an integrated legal pathway for inclusive and just societal transformation. A qualitative doctrinal methodology, complemented by analytical and comparative approaches, was adopted. The study draws on relevant legislation, judicial authorities, scholarly literature and international instruments. The study finds that digital exclusion, algorithmic bias, data privacy violations, cybercrime, platform power and inadequate digital remedies can undermine equity and justice. It further finds that Rawls’ Theory of Justice, Sen’s Capability Approach and Digital Constitutionalism provide complementary foundations for addressing these challenges, but fragmented legal responses remain inadequate. The study consequently proposes the Transformative Digital Justice Framework (TDJF), integrating constitutional rights protection, digital inclusion, responsible technology governance, digital consumer protection, institutional accountability, judicial innovation and inclusive participation. The study concludes that law must move beyond reactive regulation and proactively shape digital transformation to ensure that technological progress advances human dignity, equality, inclusion and justice. Keywords: Digital Transformation; Equity; Justice; Artificial Intelligence; Digital Rights; Consumer Protection; Digital Constitutionalism.

items.title: Reimagining HRM: Job Crafting and Artificial Intelligence as Drivers of Organizational Performance in the Public Sector
items.abstract: Organisations increasingly combine employee-led job redesign with artificial intelligence (AI) to support adaptive work and performance. This study examines the relationships among job crafting (JC), self-reported AI use, and employee-reported performance-related outcomes in the UAE public sector. Primary cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 433 employees working in HRM departments of Dubai Government organisations. The study tests the direct associations of JC and AI with the outcome measure, the moderating role of AI in the JC-outcome relationship, and whether these relationships differ formally across gender and age groups. Regression results show positive associations for JC (β = 0.552, p < 0.001) and AI use (β = 0.166, p < 0.001). The AI × JC interaction is not significant (B = −0.024, t = −0.650, p = 0.516), indicating that AI does not strengthen the JC-outcome relationship in this sample. Formal interaction tests also do not establish significant differences in the focal relationships across gender or age groups. The findings suggest that job crafting and AI use may contribute independently to perceived performance-related outcomes, while their combination is not automatically synergistic. The study contributes to human-centred AI and job-crafting research in a public-sector setting, while explicitly recognising limitations arising from convenience sampling, cross-sectional self-report data, and the restricted content validity of the retained measurement composites. From a social sustainability perspective, these findings inform how employee autonomy and responsible AI use may support adaptable public-sector work practices and sustainable human resource management. The results highlight the importance of balancing digital transformation with employee agency, while not establishing long-term sustainability outcomes.

items.title: Reorganization During Absence and Incomplete Positional Restoration: Why Coming Back Is Not the Same as Going Back
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Reorganization During Absence and Incomplete Positional Restoration, a mechanism by which a person's absence prompts others to redistribute work, responsibilities, and relations of dependence, so that returning does not automatically restore the position previously held. An individual may resume participation in an organization whose arrangements have changed to accommodate the absence. The person's return and the restoration of the former role are therefore separate events. The paper assesses positional restoration by comparing the tasks, relationships, and dependencies that constituted the earlier position with the arrangements in place upon return. It asks which responsibilities moved during the absence, who acquired them, and what would be required to reverse the redistribution. Restoration may be possible, but it requires an additional operation with consequences for those who assumed the work. The mechanism does not establish that the earlier arrangement was preferable, that the returning person is entitled to recover it, or that adaptations made during an absence are necessarily permanent. The documented case concerns New England Patriots quarterback Drew Bledsoe, who was injured during a game against the New York Jets on September 23, 2001. His replacement, Tom Brady, started the following eight games. When Bledsoe was medically cleared to return in November, head coach Bill Belichick retained Brady as the starting quarterback. Belichick explained that preparing both players had reduced the practice opportunities needed by the starter. The starting role and its associated preparation had moved during Bledsoe's absence and were not restored when he became available. A contrasting case concerns Soviet cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev, who launched to the Mir space station in May 1991 and returned in March 1992 after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. His mission was extended because a planned replacement did not assume his duties. Although his circumstances changed substantially during the absence, his assignment had not been transferred to another person and then withheld upon return. Part of the Time, Memory, and Revision series within On Human Modeling, the paper places the mechanism alongside Alfred Schutz's account of the homecomer and examines how continuity of identity differs from continuity of organizational position. Potential applications in human–AI research include organizational transitions, human–AI task allocation, workplace automation, and evaluations of whether restored access or participation also restores the responsibilities, information, and decision authority previously held by a person.

items.title: Research through evaluation for large language models in patient-clinician communications
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft replies to patient messages, but the methods available for evaluating such drafts were developed for other kinds of systems, and expert evaluators are difficult to recruit at the scale that LLM output requires. We propose Research through Evaluation (RtE), an iterative approach in which the evaluation metrics and the grading rubric are developed together with the clinicians who apply them. We applied RtE in a retrospective comparative study of 158 prostate cancer patient inquiries, comparing replies written by the clinical care team with replies generated by a GPT-4-based in-basket bot. Three rounds of human evaluation with clinical professionals (Rounds 1–3) were followed by a fourth round in which four LLM graders scored the same responses with the final rubric. Across the human rounds, the design moved from disclosed-source comparison to randomized single-blind grading, Conciseness was replaced by Clarity and Trustworthiness by Empathy, and items on editing effort and time to answer were added. In the final clinician evaluation, clinical care team replies scored higher on Completeness, Correctness and Clarity, in-basket bot replies scored higher on Empathy, and in-basket bot replies more often needed major editing. All four LLM graders rated the in-basket bot replies more favourably than the clinical care team replies, and their absolute agreement with one another was low (Krippendorff's alpha 0.07–0.18) compared with that of the clinician graders (0.53–0.81). RtE produced a documented evaluation instrument in which every revision can be traced to the round that prompted it, and the results indicate that zero-shot LLM graders cannot yet replace clinician evaluation in this setting.

items.title: Responsible AI Integration in Research: Exploring Researchers’ Information Behaviors and Ethical Decision-Making
items.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in academic work, it is reshaping how researchers seek, interpret, and use information across scholarly activities (Andersen et al., 2025). At the same time, AI-generated information presents new challenges for credibility assessment because its reliability and suitability for academic tasks are not always readily apparent (Choi et al., 2025). This study examines how generative AI is incorporated into academic information practices and how people respond when its outputs remain uncertain. The semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 faculty members, graduate students, librarians, and academic support professionals working or studying in U.S. higher-education settings. An iterative thematic analysis showed that participants rarely treated generative AI as a self-contained information source. Instead, they moved between AI systems, scholarly resources, specialised tools, and human expertise as their tasks developed. Uncertainty often emerged when generated information appeared plausible but was difficult to substantiate, when participants lacked the expertise needed to judge an answer, or when AI involvement conflicted with their understanding of appropriate academic work. Participants responded by seeking corroborating evidence, revising how AI was used within a task, or turning away from it when further checking required too much effort or when they wished to retain personal judgement and authorship. Faculty and academic support professionals also described a broader responsibility for helping students and colleagues navigate these uncertainties through clearer expectations and critical guidance. The findings position generative AI within a wider academic information environment and show that its use is shaped by continuing judgements about when generated information is sufficient, when other resources are needed, and where human responsibility should remain.

items.title: Rethinking Feedback in Higher Education: Graduate Students’ Views on Peer and GenAI Feedback
items.abstract: Amid the rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), this study investigates how integrating this technology into educational feedback processes can enhance learning experiences. Specifically, we investigate the potential of GenAI to complement peer feedback practices among 295 graduate students at a US-based university during the 2023 academic year. Employing an exploratory research design, the study gathered both quantitative and qualitative data through post-course surveys to address key research questions regarding the quality, usefulness, and actionability of peer and AI reviews, as well as their respective advantages and disadvantages. The findings reveal that, while peer reviews were slightly more favorably perceived across all dimensions, AI-generated feedback offered unique strengths, such as consistency and immediacy, which may enrich the feedback experience in distinct ways. The thematic analysis revealed distinct but complementary functions associated with each modality. This research underscores the importance of integrating human expertise with AI technology in feedback mechanisms. By illuminating how AI can augment, rather than replace, human feedback, we offer practical insights for educators, instructional designers, and policymakers seeking to enhance feedback experiences through emerging digital technologies.

items.title: Rethinking the AI Pharmakon - What Modern Medicine Has to Say to a Philosophical Figure
items.abstract: Readers of the philosophical literature on artificial intelligence (AI) will encounter an unexpected word, one that medicine has carried for two and a half millennia: pharmakon . Revitalised by Derrida and elaborated by Bernard Stiegler into a general theory of technology, the figure has lately been carried over to generative AI to capture the simultaneous enhancement and diminishment of cognition this technology produces in its users. The present paper argues that when philosophy borrows this word it should borrow it in full, in the sense it has acquired since Plato. The phármakon of contemporary clinical medicine is a relational object whose therapeutic or toxic character emerges in a specified encounter between substance, subject, and context. Stiegler’s pharmacology is itself relational, locating ambivalence in the process of transindividuation; but it does not provide an operational vocabulary for specifying how effects vary systematically between individual subjects. Clinical pharmacology provides such a vocabulary. Its accumulated learning — pharmacokinetic variability, pharmacogenetic polymorphism, idiosyncratic susceptibility, drug–drug interaction, therapeutic window, tolerance, withdrawal, and expectancy effects — has cognitive analogues in human interaction with large language models (LLMs) that have not yet been developed into a coherent pharmacological vocabulary and that early empirical research is beginning to measure. The paper proposes a reframing from the generic to the respondent pharmakon , not as a refutation of Stiegler’s pharmacology but as its specification at a level where clinical, pedagogical, and policy decisions can be made.

items.title: Retinal foundation-model versus ImageNet pretraining for deep learning grading of diabetic retinopathy: an external validation study
items.abstract: Purpose To determine whether retinal foundation-model pretraining reduces the loss of diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading agreement on external fundus-photograph datasets compared with ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks. Methods RETFound (linear probe and full fine-tuning), EfficientNet-B3 and ResNet-50 were developed on APTOS 2019 (3,662 images) and tested unchanged on Messidor-2 (1,744 images, adjudicated grades) and IDRiD (516 images). The prespecified primary outcome was the difference in internal-to-external quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) drop relative to EfficientNet-B3 for one training run per model; a post hoc analysis averaged three or four runs per model. Results Internal QWK was 0.879 (EfficientNet-B3) and 0.888 (RETFound). In the prespecified analysis, RETFound’s excess drop was + 0.020 (95% CI − 0.024 to + 0.064) on Messidor-2 and + 0.033 (− 0.023 to + 0.091) on IDRiD; averaged over runs, it was + 0.068 (+ 0.003 to + 0.134; Holm p = 0.074) and + 0.020 (− 0.041 to + 0.080). On Messidor-2, referable-DR sensitivity was 36–43% with specificity 90–98%, and EfficientNet-B3 graded 259 of 270 mild-DR images as no DR. Matching case mix and merging grades 0 and 1 reduced the Messidor-2 drop by 63–69%. Label smoothing reproduced RETFound’s lower external calibration error. Conclusion Retinal foundation-model pretraining did not reduce external performance loss. Similar internal agreement did not establish robustness across image sources and reference standards, and no model was suitable for autonomous screening at these operating points.

items.title: Rock Typing in the Digital Age: A Systematic Review of Petrophysical Foundations, Advanced Conventional Formulations, and the Ascent of Physics-Informed Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Petrophysical rock typing (PRT) is the cornerstone of reservoir characterization, bridging microscopic pore-throat morphology and macroscopic dynamic flow behavior to control hydrocarbon-in-place estimates, saturation–height functions, and numerical simulation grid-block properties. For over five decades, reservoir workflows have relied on conventional frameworks rooted in capillary pressure curves (Leverett, 1941; Thomeer, 1960), pore-throat size calibrations (Winland R₃₅; Pittman, 1992), and the modified Kozeny-Carman formulation, most notably the Reservoir Quality Index (RQI) and Flow Zone Indicator (FZI) proposed by Amaefule et al. (1993). However, these classical formulations frequently struggle in complex carbonate systems, tight gas sandstones, and multi-modal reservoirs due to fundamental physical limitations, including the conflation of static capillary storage with dynamic flow capacity, non-Darcy flow regimes, and unresolved multi-scale heterogeneity. This review systematically traces the methodological evolution of rock typing from its historical foundations to the contemporary ascent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). We first evaluate advanced conventional advancements that address classical shortcomings, including the rigorous decoupling of Petrophysical Static Rock Types (PSRT) from Petrophysical Dynamic Rock Types (PDRT), the calibration of effective flow porosity (PHIZ) via Purcell-PSKT porosimetry, and fractal bound-water models for low-permeability rocks. We then conduct an in-depth critical analysis of data-driven AI, examining how unsupervised clustering (Self-Organizing Maps, K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, DBSCAN) automates electrofacies discovery from multi-well wireline logs, and how supervised tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) and deep architectures predict rock classes and continuous permeability. Crucially, we highlight the paradigm shift toward Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML), where non-Darcy flow physics and mass conservation are embedded directly into loss functions, and Explainable AI (SHAP, LIME) is leveraged to eliminate black-box opacity. We further analyze the revolution in Digital Rock Physics (DRP) and Image-based Microscale Rock Typing (IMRT), which combines micro-CT, FIB-SEM, and deep learning segmentation (PRRT and TSRT) with Lattice Boltzmann flow simulation to provide verifiable ground truth. Finally, we replace speculative risks with an industry-grounded audit of genuine operational pitfalls in AI petrophysics — including spatial autocorrelation data leakage, out-of-distribution extrapolation failure, core-to-log depth-matching errors, and regulatory compliance — and synthesize these insights into a unified, multi-scale, physics-informed digital rock typing roadmap for resilient reservoir modeling.

items.title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
items.abstract: One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.
